newsitem.title: FRANCE: Thomson-Matra would boost European arms industry.
newsitem.headline: Thomson-Matra would boost European arms industry.

text.p: A merger of Lagardere Groupe's Matra missiles business and defence electronics firm Thomson-CSF would form the world's second-largest weapons system group, boosting the French and European defence industries, Defence Minister Charles Millon said on Wednesday.

Lagardere, whose bid to take over Thomson SA was chosen by the government over a rival offer by Alcatel Alsthom, proposed a vertical integration through the merger of Matra and Thomson-CSF -- a new entity which Lagardere would control. The government would retain a golden share out of national security interest.
"It would create the second-largest group globally in the area of weapons systems," Millon told a news conference.

He said the government's decision was part of President Jacques Chirac's aim of modernising the defence industry, beginning with the decision in February to push Dassault Aviation and state-owned Aerospatiale into a merger.

"This is particularly necessary when you see the contraction of defence budgets around the world, and the need for a modern group with the strength to compete internationally and export," Millon said.

Finance Minister Jean Arthuis said the new entity would be a leader in the industry thanks to the complementarity of the Matra and Thomson-CSF businesses. "It reinforces the European defence industry," he said.
The world's biggest defence group in terms of turnover is U.S. Lockheed Martin.

The ministers discussed the plans proposed by the bidding rivals -- Lagardere's plan for vertical integration, by strengthening the range of its defence activities, and Alcatel's plan for horizontal integration, or expansion of its activities.
"It's not that we favour one approach more than the other but a choice had to be made," Millon said.
"It's certain there are many synergies at the technological level," Industry Minister Franck Borotra told the conference. He said 20 of Matra's technologies would be reinforced through a merger.
"The solution leaves the door open to multiple cooperation accords at the European level," Borotra added.
"There is no question of creating a monopoly," Millon said. "The deal between Aerospatiale and DASA in the areas of missiles and satellites will be pursued," he said.
